title: How Crayola got its name
hook: Crayola is French chalk plus a bit of an old word for oily.
peek: When Binney and Smith launched their first box of wax crayons in 1903, a former schoolteacher in the family came up with the name. She joined the French word for chalk with part of a word meaning oily.
lede: In 1903 the Binney and Smith company of New York sold its first box of wax crayons: eight colours for a nickel. The name came from Alice Binney, the wife of co-founder Edwin Binney and a former schoolteacher. She joined craie, French for chalk, with ola, taken from oleaginous, an old word for oily. Chalky colour made with oily wax.

bullets.text: The 1903 box held black, brown, blue, red, purple, orange, yellow and green. Cheap, safe wax crayons for children were new: imported coloured crayons were costly, and the firm's own wax crayon was a black one for marking crates and barrels.

Before crayons the firm sold carbon black, a pigment used to darken car tyres, plus slate pencils for schools. Salesmen visiting classrooms heard that teachers wanted better, cheaper colours for pupils, which pushed the company toward crayons.

Schools were already customers for the company's dustless chalk, sold as An-Du-Septic, which won a gold medal at the 1904 St Louis World's Fair. Chalk was already a school staple for the firm when the crayons arrived.
The name grew so much bigger than the company that in 2007 Binney and Smith renamed itself Crayola. More than a century on, the brand still carries Alice Binney's blend of chalk and oily wax.
